:::

Describing a dataset in numbers and in pictures.
:::

:::

:::

---

## 3.1 Representing Data {#representing-data}

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Data and notation**

Data are **measurements** we write symbolically. For $n$ observations, we use a lowercase letter $x$ with a subscript for the index:

$$x_1, \; x_2, \; \ldots, \; x_n$$

where $x_i$ is one observation and $i = 1, \ldots, n$. The value $n$ is the **sample size**.
:::

<br>

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Condensed form**: $\; x_i : i = 1, \ldots, n$
:::

---

## 3.1 Tabular Form

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
| Index | 1 | 2 | $\cdots$ | $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Observation | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $\cdots$ | $x_n$ |

<br>

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Example.** Five students' study hours:

$$3, \; 4, \; 4, \; 6, \; 8$$

Here $n = 5$, $x_1 = 3$, $x_2 = 4$, $\ldots$, $x_5 = 8$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Why bother with notation?**

Once we write data as $x_1, \ldots, x_n$, every formula in this chapter (mean, variance, IQR) reads the same regardless of what the data actually measure.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Example: Commute Methods {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
A survey asked 40 STA258 students how they usually commute to campus.

| Method | Bus | Car | Walk | Train | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 14 | 9 | 5 | 8 | 4 |

**(a)** Is this variable **qualitative** or **quantitative**?

**(b)** Create a **relative frequency** table.

**(c)** Which method is most common?

**(d)** What percentage use **public transport** (Bus and Train)?
:::

---

## Commute Methods - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

freq <- c(Bus = 14, Car = 9, Walk = 5, Train = 8, Other = 4)

freq / sum(freq)                              # relative frequency
names(freq)[which.max(freq)]                  # most common
(freq["Bus"] + freq["Train"]) / sum(freq)     # transit share
```

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

A class collects the daily steps walked by ten students: $4, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12$ (thousands of steps). In the notation $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$, what is $n$?
::::

- 4
- 8
- [10]{.correct data-explanation="$n$ is the sample size — the number of observations."}
- 12

## 3.2 Numerical Measures {#numerical-measures}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Centre</span>
Where is the "typical" value? Mean, median, mode.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Spread</span>
How dispersed are the values? Variance, SD, range, IQR.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Position</span>
Where does one value sit relative to the rest? Percentiles, quartiles.
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
No single number tells the whole story. We pair centre with spread, and read both alongside a plot.
:::

---

## 3.2.1 Mean

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Sample mean** $\bar{x}$

For a sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$,

$$\bar{x} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n} \; = \; \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
The mean is the **arithmetic average** - the one most people mean when they say "average."
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

hours <- c(3, 4, 4, 6, 8)

sum(hours)        # numerator
length(hours)     # n
mean(hours)       # built-in
```
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.2 Median

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Median**

The middle value of a data set once the observations are sorted in ascending order.

Let $x_{(1)}, x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}$ be the sorted values. Then:

- If $n$ is **odd**:  $\;\;$ Median $=$ observation $\left(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\right)$
- If $n$ is **even**:  $\;\;$ Median $=$ average of observations $\left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{n}{2} + 1\right)$
:::

---

## 3.2.2 Median in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

odd_data  <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)
even_data <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9)

sort(odd_data)         # see the order
median(odd_data)       # middle value

sort(even_data)
median(even_data)      # average of the two middle values
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Sorted odd:** 1, 1, **3**, 4, 5 → middle value is 3.

**Sorted even:** 1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9 → middle pair is **3** and **4**, so median $= (3 + 4)/2 = 3.5$.
:::
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.3 Mode

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Mode**

The most frequently occurring value in a data set.

A data set can be **unimodal**, **bimodal**, or have no mode if every value appears the same number of times.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 8)

# R has no built-in mode() for the statistical mode
counts <- table(x)
counts                            # frequency of each value
names(counts)[which.max(counts)]  # the mode
```
:::
::::

---

## Example: Study Hours {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
Ten students reported the number of hours they studied for a midterm:

$$2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 9, 12$$

**(a)** Find the **mean** study time.

**(b)** Find the **median** study time.

**(c)** Find the **mode**.

**(d)** Which measure of centre is most affected by the value $12$? Explain briefly.
:::

---

## Study Hours - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 9, 12)

mean(x)
median(x)

counts <- table(x)
names(counts)[which.max(counts)]   # mode
```

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

A class has the following test scores out of 100:
$72, 75, 78, 80, 82, 85, 12$.
One student missed most of the term and scored 12. **Which measure best describes a "typical" score?**
::::

- Mean
- [Median]{.correct data-explanation="The mean is dragged down by the 12. The median (80) sits in the middle of the rest of the class and is **resistant** to that one extreme value."}
- Mode
- Range

---

## 3.2.4 Variance

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Sample variance** $s^2$

The average squared deviation from the mean:

$$s^{2} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$$

where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Each term is squared**, so $s^2 \ge 0$ always.

The **units** of $s^2$ are the units of the data **squared** (e.g. dollars²). That is awkward to interpret, which is why we usually report the standard deviation instead.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Why divide by $n-1$?

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Bessel's correction.** We use sample data $\bar{x}$ to estimate the (unknown) population mean $\mu$. That estimation step "uses up" one piece of information.

Dividing by $n - 1$ instead of $n$ corrects for this, and makes $s^2$ an **unbiased** estimator of the population variance.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
You will see a formal proof of this in **STA260**. For now, just remember:

- **Sample** variance → divide by $n - 1$
- **Population** variance → divide by $N$
:::

---

## 3.2.4 Variance in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8)

# Step by step
xbar <- mean(x)
xbar

dev  <- x - xbar          # deviations
sq   <- dev^2             # squared deviations
sum(sq) / (length(x) - 1) # variance by formula

var(x)                    # built-in (same answer)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Tip.** Build the table $(x_i, x_i - \bar{x}, (x_i - \bar{x})^2)$ on paper before reaching for `var()`. Several exam questions ask for the table.
:::
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.5 Standard Deviation

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Sample standard deviation** $s$

$$s \; = \; +\sqrt{s^{2}}$$

where $s^2$ is the sample variance.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Taking the square root returns us to the **original units**, which is why we usually report $s$ rather than $s^2$.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8)

var(x)        # variance
sd(x)         # standard deviation
sqrt(var(x))  # the same thing
```
:::
::::

---

## 3.2.6 Range

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**Range**

$$\text{Range} \; = \; \max(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \; - \; \min(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$$

The difference between the largest and smallest observations.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
**Caution.** The range uses only two values, so a single extreme observation can change it dramatically. It is a quick summary, not a robust one.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 30)

min(x)
max(x)
max(x) - min(x)   # range

range(x)          # returns min and max as a vector
diff(range(x))    # also gives the range
```
:::
::::

---

## Example: Quiz Scores {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
A student recorded their quiz scores out of $10$:

$$6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10$$

**(a)** Find the **range**.

**(b)** Find the **sample variance** $s^{2}$.

**(c)** Find the **sample standard deviation** $s$.

**(d)** What does the standard deviation tell us in this context?
:::

---

## Quiz Scores - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10)

diff(range(x))   # range
var(x)           # sample variance
sd(x)            # sample standard deviation
```

---

## 3.2.7 Percentiles

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**$p^{\text{th}}$ percentile**

In an ordered data set, the $p^{\text{th}}$ percentile is the value such that $p\%$ of all observations lie **below** it.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Example.** A class writes a difficult test and a student scores 72%. Although 72% is a B-, the test was hard. In fact, this mark sits at the **90th percentile** for this test - the student scored higher than 90% of the class.

A relative position can matter more than the raw mark.
:::

---

## 3.2.8 Quartiles

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Quartiles**

Three values that split the sorted data into four equal-size groups.

- **First quartile** $Q_1$: 25% of values below it.
- **Second quartile** $Q_2$: 50% of values below it. **This is the median.**
- **Third quartile** $Q_3$: 75% of values below it.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Quartiles are just three specific percentiles: $Q_1 = P_{25}$, $Q_2 = P_{50}$, $Q_3 = P_{75}$.
:::

---

## Interquartile Range (IQR)

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
**IQR**

$$\text{IQR} \; = \; Q_3 - Q_1$$

The width of the middle 50% of the data.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
Unlike the range, the IQR is **resistant to outliers** because the bottom 25% and top 25% of the data are ignored.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 30)

summary(x)        # min, Q1, median, mean, Q3, max
quantile(x)       # the five-number quartile breaks
IQR(x)            # Q3 - Q1
```
:::
::::

---

## Example: Final Exam Scores {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
The final exam scores for $12$ students are:

$$52, 58, 61, 65, 70, 72, 75, 78, 82, 86, 90, 96$$

**(a)** Find the **median**.

**(b)** Find the **first quartile**, $Q_{1}$.

**(c)** Find the **third quartile**, $Q_{3}$.

**(d)** Find the **interquartile range** (IQR).

**(e)** Using the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule, which scores would be flagged as unusually low or high?
:::

---

## Final Exam Scores - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(52, 58, 61, 65, 70, 72, 75, 78, 82, 86, 90, 96)

summary(x)
IQR(x)

q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25); q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75); iqr <- q3 - q1
c(lower = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr)
```

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

For a sample with $Q_1 = 5$ and $Q_3 = 11$, would an observation of $25$ be flagged as a potential outlier by the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule?
::::

- [Yes - it sits above the upper cutoff]{.correct data-explanation="IQR $= 6$, upper cutoff $= 11 + 1.5 \\times 6 = 20$. Since $25 > 20$, the value is flagged as a high outlier."}
- No - it sits inside the whiskers
- We cannot tell without the median
- We cannot tell without the sample size

---

## 3.3 Graphical Techniques {#graphical-techniques}

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Why plot at all?</span>
Numbers alone hide the **shape** of a distribution. A picture reveals skewness, gaps, clusters, and unusual values.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Two workhorses</span>
**Histograms** show the full shape of one variable. **Boxplots** highlight centre, spread, and outliers, and stack neatly for group comparisons.
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Pair numbers with pictures.** A mean of 65 looks different on a symmetric bell than on a right-skewed pile with a long tail. Always look at both.
:::

---

## Skewness

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Skewness**

A measure of the **symmetry** (or lack of it) in the distribution of data.
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Left-skewed</span>
Long tail on the **left**. Most values bunched on the right. Also called **negatively skewed**.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Symmetric</span>
Roughly mirror-image around the centre. Mean $\approx$ median.
:::
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Right-skewed</span>
Long tail on the **right**. Most values bunched on the left. Also called **positively skewed**.
:::
::::

---

## Skewness Illustrated {.compact}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

set.seed(1)
left  <- 100 - rgamma(3000, shape = 3, rate = 0.6)
sym   <- rnorm(3000, mean = 60, sd = 15)
right <- rgamma(3000, shape = 3, rate = 0.15)

df <- rbind(
  data.frame(value = left,  shape = "Left skew"),
  data.frame(value = sym,   shape = "Symmetric"),
  data.frame(value = right, shape = "Right skew")
)
df$shape <- factor(df$shape, levels = c("Left skew", "Symmetric", "Right skew"))

ggplot(df, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#9c8cd4", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ shape, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

::: {.thinkbox}
The **tail** points in the direction of the skew. "Right-skewed" = tail to the right. The mean is pulled toward the tail; the median stays near the bulk.
:::

---

## Skewness vs Mean & Median

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Rule of thumb**

- Left-skewed: **Mean $<$ Median**
- Symmetric: **Mean $\approx$ Median**
- Right-skewed: **Mean $>$ Median**

The mean is pulled toward the long tail. The median is not.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Right-skewed sample (waiting times)
set.seed(258)
wait <- rexp(200, rate = 0.1)

mean(wait)
median(wait)
# mean > median  ->  right-skewed
```
:::
::::

---

## Outliers

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Outlier**

A data point that appears to lie outside the overall pattern of the rest of the data.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Do not just delete outliers.**

Investigate first - is it a data-entry error, a measurement error, or a genuine rare observation? The right call depends on the cause.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Common causes**

- Transcription error (typing 100 instead of 10)
- Measurement error (broken instrument)
- A real but unusual case (a millionaire in a sample of incomes)
:::
:::
::::

---

## 3.3.1 Histograms

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Histogram**

A plot of a **quantitative** variable, built by:

1. Splitting the range of the data into intervals (**bins**).
2. Counting how many observations fall in each bin.
3. Drawing a bar over each bin with height equal to its frequency.

The $x$-axis shows the bins, and the $y$-axis shows frequency (or relative frequency).
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Frequency vs relative frequency.** Frequency histograms show raw counts; relative-frequency histograms show proportions (each bar height $= f_i / F$, where $F = \sum f_i$).
:::

---

## Histogram Construction {.compact}

::: {.examplebox}
**Table 3.1 - How a histogram is constructed**
:::

| Class Interval | Frequency | Relative Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| $[a_1, b_1)$ | $f_1$ | $r_1 = f_1 / F$ |
| $[a_2, b_2)$ | $f_2$ | $r_2 = f_2 / F$ |
| $[a_3, b_3)$ | $f_3$ | $r_3 = f_3 / F$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ |
| $[a_m, b_m]$ | $f_m$ | $r_m = f_m / F$ |
| **Total** | $F = \sum_{i=1}^{m} f_i$ | $1$ |

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Bin widths are usually equal** but do not have to be. We choose a width that shows the structure of the data without too much noise.
:::

---

## 3.3.1 Histogram in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

# Old Faithful eruption waiting times
data(faithful)

waiting <- faithful$waiting

hist(waiting,
     main = "Old Faithful waiting times",
     xlab = "Waiting time (minutes)",
     col  = "#00695c",
     border = "white")
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Try it.** Add the argument `breaks = 5` (or 30) to the `hist()` call to see how bin width changes the picture.

The faithful waiting times are **bimodal** - two distinct clusters around 55 and 80 minutes.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Bin Width Matters {.compact}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

data(faithful)
w <- faithful$waiting

df_b <- rbind(
  data.frame(value = w, panel = "breaks = 5"),
  data.frame(value = w, panel = "breaks = 15"),
  data.frame(value = w, panel = "breaks = 40")
)
df_b$panel <- factor(df_b$panel, levels = c("breaks = 5", "breaks = 15", "breaks = 40"))

ggplot(df_b, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(df_b, panel == "breaks = 5"),  bins = 5,  fill = "#00695c", colour = "white") +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(df_b, panel == "breaks = 15"), bins = 15, fill = "#00695c", colour = "white") +
  geom_histogram(data = subset(df_b, panel == "breaks = 40"), bins = 40, fill = "#00695c", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Waiting time (minutes)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

::: {.thinkbox}
Too few bins hide the **bimodal** shape; too many bins make it look noisy. The middle picture (15 bins) shows both clusters clearly.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

A right-skewed histogram shows the **annual salaries** at a tech company. A reporter writes: *"The average salary is \$95,000, so most employees earn around that amount."*

Which is the better summary of a **typical** employee's salary?
::::

- The mean
- [The median]{.correct data-explanation="Right-skew means a few very high salaries pull the mean above the typical value. The median sits closer to where most employees actually are."}
- They give the same answer
- Neither - use the mode

---

## 3.3.2 Boxplots

::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Boxplot** (box-and-whisker plot)

A five-number summary in graphical form:

- **Box** spans from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$.
- **Line** inside the box marks the median.
- **Whiskers** extend out to the most extreme observation **inside** the outlier cutoffs.
- **Dots** beyond the whiskers are flagged as potential outliers.
:::

---

## The $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ Rule

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
**Outlier cutoffs (fences)**

$$\text{Lower cutoff} = Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$$
$$\text{Upper cutoff} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$$

Any value outside these cutoffs is flagged as a **potential outlier**.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox .fragment}
**Example.** A dataset has $Q_1 = 5$, $Q_3 = 11$, so $\text{IQR} = 6$ and $1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 9$.

- Lower cutoff: $5 - 9 = -4$
- Upper cutoff: $11 + 9 = 20$

Any value below $-4$ or above $20$ would be flagged.
:::
:::
::::

---

## 3.3.2 Boxplot in R

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 30)

# Five-number summary
summary(x)

boxplot(x,
        horizontal = TRUE,
        main = "Bus wait times (minutes)",
        col  = "#00695c")
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**What to look for**

- Where does the median sit inside the box? Off-centre suggests skew.
- How long are the whiskers? Unequal whisker lengths also suggest skew.
- Any dots? Those are potential outliers.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Skewness from a Boxplot

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

set.seed(3)
df_box <- rbind(
  data.frame(value = 30 - rgamma(150, shape = 3, rate = 0.5),  shape = "Left skew"),
  data.frame(value = rnorm(150, mean = 10, sd = 3),            shape = "Symmetric"),
  data.frame(value = rgamma(150, shape = 3, rate = 0.5),       shape = "Right skew")
)
df_box$shape <- factor(df_box$shape, levels = c("Left skew", "Symmetric", "Right skew"))

ggplot(df_box, aes(x = value, y = shape, fill = shape)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, colour = "#004d40", outlier.colour = "#e34a6f") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#9c8cd4", "#00aa88", "#f9a825"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Value", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**Reading skew from a box.** Median **closer to $Q_3$** + long lower whisker → left skew. Median **closer to $Q_1$** + long upper whisker → right skew. The longer tail points in the direction of the skew.
:::

---

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
A professor records the time, in minutes, that students spent completing an online quiz:

$$12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 35, 42$$

**(a)** Would a **histogram** or **boxplot** better show the **shape** of the distribution?

**(b)** Would a **boxplot** or **histogram** be better for **identifying possible outliers**?

**(c)** Describe the likely **shape**: symmetric, left-skewed, or right-skewed.

**(d)** Which value seems most likely to be an outlier?
:::

## Online Quiz Times - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 35, 42)

summary(x)
hist(x, col = "#00695c", border = "white", main = NULL, xlab = "Minutes")
boxplot(x, horizontal = TRUE, col = "#00695c")
```

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

Boxplots of 80 delivery times. Restaurant **A** has a short box, short whiskers, and no outliers. Restaurant **B** has a wider box, a long upper whisker, and two high outliers. One sells sushi (careful, consistent prep), the other pizza (occasional rush orders). **Which is the sushi restaurant?**
::::

- [Restaurant A]{.correct data-explanation="Tight spread = consistent delivery. B's long upper whisker and high outliers fit pizza rush orders."}
- Restaurant B
- Both equally consistent
- Cannot tell

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

In a sample, the median sits noticeably **closer to $Q_3$** than to $Q_1$, and the **lower whisker is longer**. What does this suggest?
::::

- The distribution is right-skewed
- [The distribution is left-skewed]{.correct data-explanation="Mass is concentrated on the high side ($Q_3$ end), with a long tail to the left. Mean would be **less** than median."}
- The distribution is symmetric
- There must be a high outlier

---

## Comparing Two Groups

:::: {.two-col-lean}
::: {.col}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false

groupA <- c(14, 15, 14, 16, 15, 14, 16, 15, 15, 16)
groupB <- c( 8, 12, 15, 19, 18, 11, 17, 20, 20, 10)

mean(groupA); sd(groupA)
mean(groupB); sd(groupB)

boxplot(list(A = groupA, B = groupB),
        col = c("#00695c", "#f9a825"),
        main = "Quiz scores by group")
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
**Same mean, different stories.**

Both groups have $\bar{x} = 15$, but Group B is much more spread out. Mean alone hides this - the standard deviation and the side-by-side boxplots make it obvious.
:::
:::
::::

## Example: Two Sections {.scrollable}

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Example</span>
Two sections of a course report the following midterm marks. **Section A:** $62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78$. **Section B:** $45, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 95$.

**(a)** Find the **mean** mark for each section.

**(b)** Find the **median** mark for each section.

**(c)** Which section has more **spread**? Explain.

**(d)** For Section B, would the mean or the median better represent a typical student? Explain.
:::

---

## Two Sections - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

A <- c(62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78)
B <- c(45, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 95)

mean(A); median(A); sd(A)
mean(B); median(B); sd(B)

boxplot(list(A = A, B = B), col = c("#00695c", "#f9a825"), main = "Midterm marks")
```

---

## Worked Example: Variance Table {.compact}

::: {.examplebox}
**Six study hours**: $x = 2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8$. $\;\;\bar{x} = 30 / 6 = 5$.
:::

| $x_i$ | $x_i - \bar{x}$ | $(x_i - \bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $-3$ | $9$ |
| 4 | $-1$ | $1$ |
| 4 | $-1$ | $1$ |
| 6 | $+1$ | $1$ |
| 6 | $+1$ | $1$ |
| 8 | $+3$ | $9$ |
| **Sum** | $0$ | $22$ |

$$s^2 = \frac{22}{6 - 1} = 4.4, \quad s = \sqrt{4.4} \approx 2.10$$

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Example

A teaching assistant wants to **compare the distribution of test scores between two tutorial sections**. Which graph is best suited for this comparison?
::::

- A bar chart
- Two separate histograms
- [Side-by-side boxplots]{.correct data-explanation="Boxplots stack cleanly for group comparison and show centre, spread, and outliers at once. Histograms work but are harder to compare side by side."}
- A scatterplot

---

## Chapter Summary {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Centre</span>
**Mean** uses every value. **Median** ignores extremes. **Mode** is the most common value.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Spread</span>
**Range** = max − min (sensitive). **IQR** = $Q_3 - Q_1$ (resistant). **SD** $s$ is the typical distance from $\bar{x}$.
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Shape</span>
Read **skewness** from a histogram (which way does the tail point?) or a boxplot (which whisker is longer?).
:::
::::

<br>

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** Always report a number **and** a picture. A mean without a histogram, or a histogram without a summary, leaves half the story untold.
:::

---

::: {.taskbox}
<span class="label">Bonus Example</span>
The number of textbooks owned by $15$ students:

$$0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10$$

**(a)** Is the variable **discrete** or **continuous**?

**(b)** Find the **mean**, **median**, and **mode**.

**(c)** Find the **range** and the **IQR**.

**(d)** Would a **histogram** or **boxplot** better show the overall shape?

**(e)** Would a **boxplot** or **histogram** be more useful for detecting outliers?
:::

## Bonus Example: Textbooks Owned - Check in R

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

x <- c(0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10)

mean(x); median(x)
table(x)                   # mode = most frequent
diff(range(x)); IQR(x)

hist(x, col = "#00695c", border = "white", main = NULL, xlab = "Textbooks")
boxplot(x, horizontal = TRUE, col = "#00695c")
```
